_metadata.description: Orbit types catalog with real spacecraft examples and physical characteristics
sources: Larson, W. J., & Wertz, J. R. (Eds.). (1999). Space Mission Engineering: The New SMAD. Microcosm Press.
Vallado, D. A. (2013). Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications (4th ed.). Microcosm Press.
Curtis, H. D. (2013). Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students (3rd ed.). Butterworth-Heinemann.
ITU Radio Regulations — GEO arc filings

orbit_types.name: LEO — Low Earth Orbit
orbit_types.description: The most common orbit for spacecraft, ranging from the edge of significant atmosphere (~160 km) to the inner Van Allen radiation belt (~2 000 km). Shortest orbital periods, easiest to reach, but subject to atmospheric drag decay.

physical_characteristics.atmospheric_drag: Significant below 500 km; negligible above 800 km
physical_characteristics.radiation: Below inner Van Allen belt — relatively benign
physical_characteristics.eclipse_fraction: ~35% of orbit in Earth shadow at 400 km
physical_characteristics.ground_track_coverage: Global coverage with sufficient inclination and multiple satellites

advantages: Low launch energy required (ΔV ≈ 9.3–9.4 km/s from equator)
Short communication delays (2–10 ms one-way)
Earth observation with high resolution possible
Easy to service or resupply (ISS servicing missions)
disadvantages: Orbital decay due to atmospheric drag (requires periodic reboost below ~600 km)
No continuous coverage of a fixed point (passes overhead for only ~10 min)
Many satellites needed for continuous global coverage (constellations)
uses: Human spaceflight — ISS, Tiangong, future commercial stations
Broadband constellations — Starlink, OneWeb, Amazon Kuiper

real_examples.name: ISS (ZARYA)
real_examples.notes: Orbital maintenance reboosts ~4–8 times/year to counteract drag

real_examples.name: Hubble Space Telescope
real_examples.notes: Above bulk of atmosphere; natural decay ~50 years from last servicing

real_examples.name: Starlink-1007
real_examples.notes: Autonomous de-orbit capability; designed to deorbit within 5 years if active system fails

orbit_types.j2_raan_precession_rate: Varies with inclination: 0 at 90°, maximum at 0°; ~7°/day at 28°, ~5°/day at 52°

orbit_types.name: MEO — Medium Earth Orbit
orbit_types.description: Between LEO and GEO, MEO is home to the navigation satellite constellations (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou) at ~20 000 km. Longer periods, full global coverage from ~24 satellites.

physical_characteristics.radiation: Crosses outer Van Allen belt — significant proton/electron flux; shielding required

advantages: Global navigation coverage with modest constellation size (~24–30 satellites)
Lower launch energy than GEO
Moderate communication delays
disadvantages: Van Allen radiation belt exposure limits satellite lifetimes

real_examples.name: GPS IIF-10 (PRN 08)
real_examples.notes: GPS constellation uses 24 operational satellites in 6 orbital planes, 4 per plane

real_examples.name: Galileo-FOC-1 (GSAT0201)
real_examples.notes: Europe's GNSS — 30 satellites in 3 orbital planes at 56° inclination

BeiDou.notes: BeiDou-3 MEO + GEO + IGSO mixed constellation

orbit_types.name: GEO — Geostationary Orbit
orbit_types.description: A circular equatorial orbit at 35 786 km where the orbital period equals Earth's sidereal rotation period (23 h 56 min 4 s). The satellite appears stationary relative to Earth's surface.

physical_characteristics.radiation: Above Van Allen belts — high energy particle environment
physical_characteristics.delta_v_to_reach_km_s: ~4.2 GTO injection + 1.8 GEO circularisation ≈ ~6 total above LEO

advantages: Permanently visible from 40% of Earth's surface — ideal for continuous regional coverage
No tracking antennas required for ground stations
Entire ocean/continent in single field of view for weather/communications
No revisit scheduling needed
disadvantages: Large latency (240 ms) unsuitable for low-latency applications
Expensive and energy-intensive to reach (large ΔV)
GEO arc is crowded — ITU coordination required

real_examples.name: GOES-16
real_examples.notes: GOES-East at 75.2°W — primary US East Coast + Atlantic weather satellite

real_examples.name: GOES-18
real_examples.notes: GOES-West at 137°W — primary US West Coast + Pacific weather satellite

real_examples.name: Intelsat 37e
real_examples.notes: High-throughput commercial communications satellite covering Africa and Europe

graveyard_orbit.description: Satellites at end-of-life are raised 300+ km above GEO to the 'graveyard belt' to clear the valuable GEO arc per ITU regulations.

orbit_types.name: HEO — Highly Elliptical Orbit
orbit_types.description: Highly elliptical orbits with low perigee and very high apogee. The satellite spends most of its orbital time near apogee (Kepler's second law), providing long dwell over a region. The 63.4° Molniya inclination is the critical inclination where J2 causes no argument-of-perigee precession.

physical_characteristics.radiation: Passes through both Van Allen belts twice per orbit

advantages: Long dwell times over high latitudes (8 h out of 12 h)
Better polar coverage than GEO
Useful for northern hemisphere communications where GEO elevation is low
disadvantages: Coverage requires constellation of 3+ satellites for continuous service
uses: Science missions avoiding radiation belts (INTEGRAL, XMM-Newton)

critical_inclination.description: At 63.4° inclination, the J2 zonal harmonic produces equal and opposite rates in the secular drift of argument of perigee, causing it to remain frozen. This keeps the apogee over the northern hemisphere permanently.

real_examples.name: Molniya 3-50
real_examples.notes: Classic Molniya orbit design for Russian high-latitude communications

real_examples.name: INTEGRAL
real_examples.notes: Orbit chosen to spend maximum time above Van Allen belts for clean gamma-ray observations

orbit_types.name: SSO — Sun-Synchronous Orbit
orbit_types.description: A retrograde near-polar orbit where the J2 oblateness effect causes the orbital plane to precess ~0.9856°/day eastward, exactly matching Earth's annual orbital motion around the Sun. This keeps the angle between the orbital plane and the Sun-Earth line constant — passing over any location at the same local solar time every day.

physical_characteristics.atmospheric_drag: Moderate — orbital maintenance may be required

advantages: Consistent illumination conditions for optical Earth observation
Near-polar inclination gives global coverage
Regular revisit at predictable local time — ideal for change detection
disadvantages: Retrograde orbit requires slightly more ΔV than prograde
Coverage gaps at poles (true polar satellites go to ~90°+)
uses: Optical Earth observation (Sentinel-2, Landsat, SPOT, Planet)

sso_condition.description: For a given altitude, solve for retrograde inclination i such that RAAN precession rate = 0.9856°/day (Earth's mean motion around the Sun).

real_examples.name: NOAA-20 (JPSS-1)
real_examples.notes: Wide-swath VIIRS instrument provides daily global coverage

orbit_types.name: Polar Orbit
orbit_types.description: Orbits with inclination near 90°, passing over (or near) both poles. Earth rotates beneath the satellite, allowing complete global coverage every ~14 orbits (~24 hours). Not to be confused with SSO (which is retrograde and uses J2 precession).
advantages: True global coverage including poles
Rapid complete Earth coverage (24 hours)
Useful for scientific missions needing polar data

real_examples.name: GRACE Follow-On-A
real_examples.notes: Measures Earth gravity field variations using satellite-to-satellite ranging

real_examples.name: GOCE
real_examples.notes: Extremely low orbit (255 km) for high-resolution gravity gradiometry; ion thrusters compensated drag

orbit_types.name: Lagrange Point Orbits
orbit_types.description: Orbits around the Sun-Earth or Earth-Moon system Lagrange points. L1 (1.5M km sunward) and L2 (1.5M km anti-Sun) are semi-stable — small station-keeping burns maintain halo or Lissajous orbits. These are not true Keplerian orbits around Earth.

L1.location: 1.501×10⁶ km from Earth toward Sun (0.01 AU)

L2.location: 1.501×10⁶ km from Earth away from Sun (0.01 AU)
uses: Deep-space observatories needing stable thermal environment

L4_L5.location: 60° ahead/behind Earth in its orbit (at 1 AU)
missions: No human-built satellites yet; proposed for space telescopes and solar weather monitoring

real_examples.name: James Webb Space Telescope
real_examples.notes: Launched Ariane 5; L2 insertion burn Dec 24 2021; full operations Jun 2022. 10-year nominal mission.

real_examples.name: SOHO
real_examples.notes: Operated since 1996 — far exceeds original 2-year design life. Provides 24/7 solar wind data.

real_examples.name: Gaia
real_examples.notes: ESA astrometry mission mapping >1.8 billion stars. Lissajous orbit keeps it away from Earth's shadow.
